title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Word order is the English one — subject, verb, then the rest — so a plain statement comes out in the order you already think in.
You give your name with je m'appelle — literally "I call myself". The little pronoun in the middle says whose name it is: je m'appelle · vous vous appelez.

être is the one verb "to be", and it does every job English's "be" does: who you are, where you are from, and where a thing is. The ending names the person — je suis · vous êtes · il/elle est — and it is irregular, so it is learned rather than built.
After être a profession or a role stands bare: Je suis étudiant, never Je suis un étudiant. un comes back only when something describes the noun (Je suis un bon étudiant).

Every noun has a gender and its article shows it: le (m) · la (f) · les (plural, both genders). Learn each noun with its article — the ending of the noun is a hint at best, and le musée and la main both break the obvious guess.

French keeps the article where English drops it: a whole class of thing takes le, la or les. J'aime le café is "I like coffee", not "I like the coffee", and J'aime café is not a shorter sentence — it is not a sentence.

je shortens to j' in front of a vowel and the two are written as one word: j'aime, never je aime. The apostrophe belongs to je, not to the verb — with a name as the subject nothing shortens, so it is Anne aime.

An adjective agrees with the SUBJECT — whoever or whatever the sentence is about, not whoever is speaking: Marc est français · Anne est française. The written -e is often audible too: it wakes the silent consonant in front of it.
French writes the subject pronoun every time, exactly as English does: je is never dropped.

words.cue: my name is · to be called
words.note: s'appeler, "to call oneself". The little pronoun in the middle says whose name it is: je m'appelle (mine) · vous vous appelez (yours). This, and not mon nom est, is how a name is given.
A man's name. Names carry over unchanged — swap in your own.

sentences.trap: Mon nom est Marc is the English sentence translated word for word. It is grammatical, and it is not how anyone introduces themselves.
sentences.sound: Three syllables: zhuh ma-PEL. The j of je is the soft sound in the middle of "measure", the double l is a plain l, and the final -e is silent.

variations.changed: swap the name — je m'appelle itself never changes
me → vous: the same verb, turned to the person you are speaking to
a full noun can be the subject — l'étudiant, and s'appelle gives his name

mistake.why: No est — m'appelle is already the verb. Je m'appelle Marc is the whole sentence.

sentences.usage: First introductions, to anyone at all.
sentences.mnemonic: appeler is to call. Your name is what you call yourself, so je m'appelle.

words.note: I. French writes the subject pronoun every time, exactly as English does, and never drops it. In front of a vowel it shortens to j' (j'aime).

être — the one French verb "to be". It covers who you are (je suis étudiant), where you are from (je suis de Paris) and, later, where a thing is (le livre est sur la table): French makes no second choice the way some languages do. The ending names the person: suis (I) · êtes (you) · est (he, she, it). It is also the verb that builds the past of a few movement verbs, in L1-M5.

One small word doing several English jobs: "from" after an origin (je suis de Paris), "of" inside a quantity (un kilo de riz), and the "of" inside the longer prepositions (à côté de la table). It is also the bare de that replaces du, de la, un and une after a negation — je ne veux pas de café.
City names carry over, capital and all — and they take no article after de: de Paris, de Lyon.

sentences.trap: English can shrink "I am" to "I'm" and lean on it. French shrinks nothing here and drops nothing either: Je de Paris is not a shorter sentence, it is not a sentence.
sentences.sound: suis is one syllable, swee, with the final -s silent. de is a short uh. Paris ends in a silent -s: pa-REE.

variations.changed: swap the place — je suis de … is the frame
suis → est: the same verb, a different person
suis → êtes, and a rising voice turns the same words into a question

mistake.why: A city name takes no article after de: de Paris, de Lyon, de Delhi.

sentences.usage: Where you are from — the second line of any introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: suis sounds like "swee": one small word carrying the whole of "I am".

sentences.glossEn: lit. "I am student" — there is no word for "a"

words.note: student. A woman writes étudiante, and here the extra -e is not silent: it wakes the final -t, so étudiant ends on the vowel and étudiante ends on a t. Like every job after être, it stands bare.

sentences.trap: English needs "a" in front of a job — "I am a student". French leaves it out after être, and Je suis un étudiant is exactly what English pushes you to write. un comes back only once something describes the noun: Je suis un bon étudiant.
sentences.sound: Three syllables, ay-tü-DYAHN, and the final -t is silent. The é is a clean "ay" with no glide sliding off it.

variations.changed: swap the job — the missing article stays missing
est for a third person, and the -e that marks a woman
êtes for the person you are speaking to, and a rising voice makes it a question

mistake.why: No un in front of a bare job after être. It comes back only when something describes the noun: Je suis un bon étudiant.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do — a job, a course of study, a role.
sentences.mnemonic: A job after être stands on its own: suis étudiant, not suis un étudiant.

words.note: French, the adjective. It agrees with the subject: français for a man, française for a woman — and the -e is audible, turning the silent final -s into a z. The adjective is lowercase; only the noun for the person, un Français, takes a capital.

sentences.trap: English writes "French" with a capital whether it means the people, the language or the adjective. French capitalises only the person: je suis français describes me, un Français is a Frenchman, and le français is the language.
sentences.sound: Two syllables, frahn-SEH, and the final -s is silent. The ç is a plain s sound, never a k.

variations.changed: est and the feminine -e — which also wakes the final -s into a z
swap the nationality — the frame and the agreement are unchanged
êtes for the person you are speaking to, and the question is the rising voice

mistake.why: Lowercase for the adjective. The capital belongs to the noun un Français, a Frenchman — je suis français is describing myself, not naming a nation.

sentences.mnemonic: The person gets the capital, the description does not.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "I like the coffee" — French keeps the article English drops

words.note: aimer, to like. je shortens to j' in front of the vowel and the two are written as one word — j'aime, never je aime — so this is a single word to look up. The apostrophe belongs to je: with a name as the subject nothing shortens, and the verb stands alone as aime.
the, in front of a masculine noun: le café, le livre. Every noun has a gender and its article is where you see it — le (m), la (f), les (plural). Learn each noun with its article.
coffee — masculine, so le café. The same word names the place you drink it in.

sentences.trap: English says "I like coffee" with nothing in front of coffee. French will not: a whole class of thing takes le, la or les. J'aime café is the sentence an English speaker writes first, and it is not French.
sentences.sound: J'aime is one syllable, zhem — the j is the soft sound in the middle of "measure". café takes its stress on the last syllable: ka-FAY.

variations.changed: a feminine noun takes la — the article follows the noun's gender
a name as the subject: there is no je, so nothing shortens and the verb is aime
aimez for the person you are speaking to — and the English "do" has nothing to translate into

mistake.why: A kind of thing keeps its article in French: j'aime le café. Dropping it is the English habit, not a shortcut.

sentences.usage: Saying what you like — the third line of an introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: In French you like THE coffee, all of it: j'aime le café.

words.note: the, in front of a feminine noun: la musique, la maison. It is le's twin, wearing the gender of the noun behind it.

sentences.trap: There is nothing about musique that looks feminine and nothing about café that looks masculine. The gender is a fact about the word, learned with its article, and English offers no clue at all.
sentences.sound: mü-ZEEK — the u is the tight French u, lips rounded as if for oo while the tongue says ee. The final -e is silent.

variations.changed: a name as the subject — aime, with no je to shorten
aimez for the person you are speaking to, said as a question
an adjective comes AFTER the noun in French, and agrees with it

mistake.why: musique is feminine, so it takes la. The article is not a choice — it belongs to the noun.

sentences.usage: Likes and tastes, in any conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: la musique, le café — the little word carries the gender, so learn it with the noun.

words.note: the, in front of any plural noun: les livres, les cafés. One form for both genders — the plural is the one place where the gender stops showing.
book. The plural adds a written -s that is not pronounced, so le livre and les livres differ in speech only in the article.

sentences.trap: English hears its plural: "book" and "books" are two different sounds. French does not — livre and livres are one sound, and it is les that carries the plural to the ear. A learner who only listens has to listen to the little word.
sentences.sound: LEE-vruh, with the final -e barely there and the -s silent. les is "lay", not "lez" — its s only wakes up in front of a vowel.

variations.changed: les → le: one particular book, not books in general
a name as the subject — aime, with nothing shortened
aimez for the person you are speaking to, said as a question

mistake.why: The article carries the plural too: les livres. le beside a plural noun is the one place the eye catches what the ear cannot.

sentences.usage: A taste in general — books, films, a kind of thing.
sentences.mnemonic: The -s is for the eye; les is for the ear.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Marc is journalist" — there is no word for "a"

words.note: journalist. One spelling for a man and a woman — un journaliste, une journaliste — so only the article ahead of it would change. Like étudiant, it stands bare after être.

sentences.trap: est is the same verb as suis — French has no second "to be" hiding behind it. What changed is the ending, and it changed because the subject did: je suis, Marc est.
sentences.sound: est is just "eh" — the -s and the -t are both silent. journaliste ends on a clear -st: zhoor-na-LEEST.

variations.changed: the same word for a woman — only an article in front of it would change
est → suis: the ending follows the subject back to me
swap what follows être — a nationality instead of a job

mistake.why: No un in front of a bare job after être: Marc est journaliste.

sentences.mnemonic: One verb, three endings: je suis, vous êtes, il est.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Anne is French" — with the feminine ending

words.note: A woman's name. Names carry over unchanged — swap in your own.

sentences.trap: The ending follows the SUBJECT, not the speaker. A man saying this about Anne still writes française, because Anne is who the sentence is about.
sentences.sound: frahn-SEZ — the -e at the end wakes the -s into a z. Anne is one syllable, "ann", with its final -e silent.

variations.changed: a man as the subject — the -e goes, and the final -s falls silent again
suis for me, and the -e because of who I am
swap the adjective for a job — the -e marks the woman either way

mistake.why: The ending agrees with the subject, and the subject is Anne: française.

sentences.mnemonic: Look at who the sentence is about, then write the ending.

words.note: likes — the same verb as j'aime, standing on its own because the subject is a name and not je. The apostrophe in j'aime belongs to je: it is je that shortens in front of a vowel, never the verb.

sentences.trap: English changes the verb for a third person — "I like" but "she likes". French writes aime for je, for il and for elle alike; only j'aime looks different, and that is the elision, not the person.
sentences.sound: Anne aime runs together as a-NEM: French links a final consonant straight into the vowel that follows it.

variations.changed: je as the subject — and je + aime is written j'aime
a different name and a different noun; aime does not move
a plural after the verb — les, and an -s the ear does not hear

mistake.why: j' is je — "I". With Anne as the subject there is no je to shorten: Anne aime la musique.

sentences.mnemonic: j' is je in a hurry. No je, no apostrophe.
